newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU parliament to seek to change takeover bids plan.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament to seek to change takeover bids plan.

text.p: The European Parliament will try to secure changes this week to proposed framework rules on takeover bids in the European Union, which have also met opposition from Britain's voluntary takeover panel.

The proposal by the European Commission, which aims essentially to ensure the protection of minority shareholders, is the second and more modest attempt to adopt single rules on takeovers -- a plan almost 10 years old.

The new proposal for a directive leaves out well entrenched corporate anti-takeover defences and accepts that self-regulating bodies such as the UK takeover panel are just as able to preserve small investors' rights as proper legislation.

But that has failed to address the concerns of the takeover panel which has been lobbying hard for a non-binding resolution instead fearing that a directive would encourage disgruntled parties to engage in tactical litigation.
The new draft, adopted by the Commission in 1995, provides a set of guidelines and principles for the conduct and transparency of takeovers, but leaves EU states the choice of how best to meet them.
Unlike in the 1989 proposal, the Commission no longer makes it compulsory for a party which has acquired one third of the voting rights in a target company to bid for 100 percent of the shares.
The parliament, which has a strong say on legislation affecting the EU's border-free market, looks set to give broad support to the new aproach, but the devil is in the details.

A report drafted by MEP Nicole Fontaine on behalf of the EP's committee on legal affairs proposes that provisions to protect minority shareholders be triggered "as a result of an immediate or short-term acquisition" of control of a company. This is to avoid legal uncertainty when the acquisition of a company's shares does not take place in a single operation.

More importantly, the parliament is likely to set strong guidelines on the information to be provided to employees of a target company, reflecting the belief that takeovers often result in job losses.

The report proposes that employees or their representives be informed within 24 hours of the bid being made public. It also requires the bidder to inform of any "changes to the terms and conditions of employment and any envisaged dismissals".
In another key modification, the report says that the board of a target company shall consult with the employees before setting out its opinion on the bid.

Finally, the report suggests that where national legislation provides for a mandatory bid as a means to protect small shareholders, the bid shall be launched for all shares or at least 70 percent of them. In contrast the wording in Commission's proposal says that the bid shall be launched to all shareholders or 'a substantial part'.

The parliament will vote on Thursday and will give the proposal a second reading after EU ministers, usually those in charge of industry or European affairs, reach a common position on the issue. It is unclear when this will happen given that government experts have yet to meet for the first time despite having received the proposal more than 18 months ago.
